opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think I weighed it very carefully at all, which in retrospect was probably for the best. Back then neural networks had this wonderful, slightly forbidden quality. There was a burst of excitement around backpropagation and the parallel distributed processing work, and as a student it just felt like one of the most beautiful ideas around: that you could get something resembling learning out of these simple units wired together.

But I also remember a pretty clear sense from the people around me that this was not where you'd build a career. The systems were tiny, the computers were slow, and a lot of serious people thought the whole thing was a bit of a dead end, or at least something that had already been oversold once. So my takeaway was roughly: this is fascinating, I'm going to keep thinking about it, but I probably shouldn't bet my livelihood on it.

So I drifted toward mathematics and later toward visualization and design, which turned out to be wonderful in its own right. And there's a funny irony there, because a lot of what I learned about making complex systems visible and understandable ended up being exactly what's useful now for looking inside neural networks. It felt like a detour at the time, but in hindsight it was more like I was gathering tools for coming back.

If there's a lesson, it's probably that you shouldn't throw away an idea you love just because the timing seems wrong. Keep it on a back burner. Sometimes the world catches up.

r001.rationale: He says people around him viewed neural networks as a possible dead end, so he decided not to bet his livelihood on them and drifted toward mathematics and later visualization and design.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, to be honest, I don't think I weighed it very carefully at all, which is maybe the most accurate answer. I was a math student, and I came across neural networks almost by accident. This was the mid-to-late eighties, right around when backpropagation was getting rediscovered and there was this little burst of excitement. And I just found the ideas beautiful. The notion that you could have these simple units, connect them up, and get something that learned from examples instead of being programmed explicitly felt almost magical to me.

But I should be clear about the context. If you talked to most serious people in computer science or math at the time, the attitude toward neural networks ranged from polite skepticism to outright dismissal. The Minsky and Papert critique of perceptrons was still very much in the air. The feeling was that this was a field that had been tried and had failed, and that the real action was elsewhere, in symbolic AI or in more classical statistics. So if you were thinking about career prospects, it was not an obvious bet.

I remember having a kind of split feeling. On one hand, I had the sense that this was a deep idea that wasn't going away. On the other hand, I could see that the practical results were pretty underwhelming. You'd train a tiny network on a toy problem and it would sort of work, and you'd think, well, this is cute, but is it going to do anything real? Computers were slow, data was scarce, and nobody really had a theory of why these things worked when they did.

So what I ended up doing was not making a clean decision. I went off and did other things, mathematics, then journalism, then visualization, and the neural network interest just sat there as something I kept in the back of my mind. I think of it as having a long dormant period rather than a career choice. And in a way I was lucky, because when things really took off in the 2010s, I had this old affection for the subject and a lot of other skills I'd picked up along the way that turned out to be relevant to understanding what these models were actually doing.

If there's a lesson, maybe it's that you don't always have to resolve the tension between enthusiasm and practicality in the moment. Sometimes you can just hold onto an idea you love and wait for the world to catch up. Though I'd admit that's easier to say in hindsight than it felt at the time.

r001.rationale: The response says neural networks had uncertain career prospects and that Wattenberg later pursued other fields, but it describes this as no clean decision and a dormant interest. It does not clearly say he chose other work because he feared neural networks were a career dead end.

astra-6.text: I was drawn to the intellectual question: how could a network of simple elements learn something complicated? That seemed exciting in its own right. But being excited about a subject and seeing a clear career in it were different things. At the time, neural networks didn’t look like an obvious professional path. So there was a tension between following that curiosity and finding work where I could see a way forward. It certainly wasn’t a calculation that this was going to become a huge industry.

So I followed my interest in mathematics, where I could see a more established path, and kept that curiosity about neural networks in the background. Looking back, of course, it’s funny how much those prospects changed.
